item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: NOOSHEEN HASHEMI: America's AI leadership needs more than one man
item.description: Nvidia's board says it won't reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, leaving founders and co-investors waiting to learn which AI funding rounds it will still lead.
item.content:encoded:
America’s AI industry is about to find out how much of its financing depended on Jensen Huang’s word.

Huang has said he would be willing to return to Nvidia. On Tuesday, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. For independent companies raising money now, the question is whether Nvidia will still commit early enough to bring other investors into their rounds.
According to PitchBook, rounds Nvidia joined accounted for 27.2% of global venture deal value through mid-November. That includes every investor’s contribution, and a handful of very large rounds drove much of the total. Nvidia separately reported $99 billion in equity investments as of July 26. That was the value of its holdings at the time. We don’t know how much Nvidia put into independent open-model developers or how often it led their rounds.

Reflection AI shows what Nvidia could do when it chose to lead. Huang reportedly committed Nvidia to half of Reflection’s initial $1 billion target and urged other investors to join. The round grew to $2 billion, and Nvidia put in about $800 million. It was an unusually large deal. The sequence is important: Huang committed Nvidia’s money first, then brought other investors in. Nvidia stood to sell chips to Reflection, and that kind of financing deserves scrutiny. It also shows why a lead investor’s decision can
shape a round.

Nvidia still has the means to invest. On Tuesday it reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year earlier. Its board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is scrutinizing future investments, commitments and guarantees. She also said Nvidia had made no change to the financing conditions on its existing agreements with specialist cloud providers. I expect Nvidia to be more selective about taking new risks. The question for founders and co-investors is which deals it will still lead and how quickly it will decide.

JENSEN HUANG’S NVIDIA DEBACLE REVEALS AMERICA’S REAL PROBLEM: NO SKILLED BUILDERS

As an AI founder and investor, I see how quickly a delay can become a problem for a smaller company. Microsoft, Meta and Google can fund much of their own expansion. An independent lab can have paying
customers and still need to raise money to train its next model. A specialist cloud provider has to finance the chips before it can sell the computing time. If the lead investor waits, others can wait too. The company still has to decide whether it can afford to reserve the computing capacity or keep the people it hired to do the work.

China is already competing for the customers those companies could serve. The Lowy Institute counted nearly 1.8 billion downloads of Chinese models on Hugging Face in the third quarter, compared with 500 million for American models. Huawei shows customers how to run Alibaba’s Qwen on its Ascend chips. As more developers use Qwen, Huawei has a chance to sell them the systems that run it. Beijing’s AI action plan promotes both open-source cooperation and computing infrastructure abroad. That combination could become the next chapter of China’s Digital Silk Road.

BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN

Governments that want to run AI on their own infrastructure should have a competitive American choice in models and hardware. That means Nvidia and AMD, Broadcom’s custom accelerators and systems from specialists such as Cerebras and d-Matrix. Once a government buys the equipment, adapts its software and trains its engineers, switching suppliers is expensive. Americans can disagree about which chips Nvidia should be allowed to sell to China. Weakening Nvidia or the American companies that build with its technology would give Beijing an advantage while other countries are making those choices.

Nvidia should continue backing independent AI companies. Kress and Jones should tell founders and co-investors who can approve pending deals, when decisions will come and whether Nvidia intends to provide follow-on financing. Institutional investors, sovereign wealth funds and independent venture firms should start putting together rounds of their own. Elon Musk, who has welcomed the idea of hiring Huang, could bring investors together for one such partnership. It would need firm capital commitments and the freedom to make investment decisions independently of xAI and his other companies. If we make a model’s weights public, Beijing can get them too. Our allies also need American models they can run on their own infrastructure, with their own data and under their own rules. If we leave that market to China, we make it easier for Beijing to sell the systems those countries will depend on for years. Before taxpayers guarantee financing for an open-model project, an independent review should establish which U.S. security interest it serves and whether the benefits of releasing the weights justify the risks.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

I believe private investors should decide which companies deserve their money. I would make a narrow exception when a documented financing gap threatens a viable project vital to national security. The Treasury should convene private investors this week to find out which projects are at risk and how much private capital is ready to move. I would set an initial target of $100 billion in combined public and private commitments. Congress should act urgently to authorize a temporary federal credit guarantee under bipartisan oversight, drawing on the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital. Congress should
separately cap taxpayer exposure and set an expiration date. An independent committee should apply published criteria, require recusals for conflicts and approve guarantees only where private investors keep their own capital at risk.

If Nvidia and private investors fill the gaps, the guarantees can go unused. It could take months to learn which deals will proceed. A lab can lose the team it took years to assemble in weeks. Nvidia can give founders answers now, and the Treasury can bring investors together while there are still deals to do.
Disclosure: The author has an indirect investment in Reflection AI through her limited-partner interest in a fund managed by 1789 Capital.

item.title: War against data centers is costing local communities millions of dollars
item.description: A blocked $5 billion data center at Landover Mall could have helped cut Prince George's County's $130 million deficit, as vacant lots could fund schools and roads.
item.content:encoded:
Affordability and data centers were on the ballot this November. Voters made it clear that they are concerned about both issues: prices are too high and the neighborliness of data centers is in doubt. In a time of economic turbulence, cities and counties are struggling to pay for schools, roads and public safety without the tax revenue data centers generate. Where can part of the solution to affordability and concerns with data centers be found? Vacant lots.

Vacant lots can host data centers that are well maintained, comply with local architectural requirements, have security and bring in much-needed cash for local projects. An eyesore and security problem can become a revenue generator and a secure property. However, some are determined to keep data centers from developing the local economy and unsightly properties at any cost.

In early November, an activist helped block the development of a $5 billion data center that was set to break ground in the next year or so. The data center was supposed to be built on the site of Landover Mall, which closed in 2002. The vacant lot is now overgrown with grass and weeds, stretching across nearly 90 acres in Landover, Md.

AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Prince George's County, home to the former mall, is facing a $130 million budget deficit. It has lost a Six Flags amusement park, is losing the Washington Commanders to Washington, D.C., and has suffered thousands of federal job losses. Developers projected about $53.5 million a year in local tax revenue if the data center were to be built.

The activist, Taylor Frazier McCollum, isn't moved by those numbers or how they help her neighbors. "Money is, you know, a made-up concept," she said. "We buy into it every day, and we choose that this has value and this doesn't have value and to me the environment has the highest and utmost value and I need to honor that in any way."

INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE'

The rejection of a project to help revitalize a site that sorely needs it and fill the county's coffers perfectly encapsulates the political debate around data centers. Too often, proposed data centers receive automatic opposition from activists and politicians. As a result, some of America's most vulnerable and desperate communities are losing millions of dollars in tax revenue that could fund schools, fix roads, pay emergency responders and more.

Landover Mall is sadly not the only example. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects across the country worth approximately $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026, which Data Center Watch describes as the largest single-quarter total on record. That's roughly as much as all of 2025, in just three months.

HOW AMERICA CAN WIN THE AI RACE WITHOUT BURNING VOTERS

In Virginia, Prince William County stands to miss out on as much as $400 million in projected annual tax revenue following the collapse of Digital Gateway, once billed as one of the largest data center complexes in the world. The county had approved the project, but courts invalidated its rezoning approvals. The remaining developer withdrew its legal challenge in July 2026, effectively ending the plans.

On the other hand, communities that are looking to the future and allowing data centers are reaping the benefits. Virginia’s Loudoun County has embraced data centers, which have generated 38% of general fund revenue in the county’s FY2026 budget. That revenue has helped the county lower its real property tax rate every year for a decade, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026. That's real money back in homeowners' pockets. That is revenue its neighbor, Prince William County, is missing out on.

HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF

In Henrico County, Virginia, data center tax revenue pays for an Affordable Housing Trust Fund that helps first-time homebuyers with down payments. A single mother working toward a nursing degree said her new mortgage costs less than her old rent. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's data center expansion helped the parish pay for $50,000 teacher bonuses.

THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO

Data center developers have a responsibility to communities: listen to their concerns, be transparent and collaborative about their plans, design in ways their neighbors approve and work to mitigate or eliminate undesirable local impacts. They must also pay their own electric and water costs, establish noise limits and continually work with local community groups and elected officials to address concerns as they arise.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Data center development can be and often is a win-win for developers and the community. But even these efforts are not enough for some. Money may be a "made-up concept" to some, but the lower tax rates in Loudoun County, the down payment in Henrico and the teacher bonuses in Richland Parish are real.

Data centers can turn a decades-long vacant parking lot overgrown with weeds into an economic engine, helping to close a $130 million hole in the budget. Immovable opponents are ignoring the economic benefits data centers can bring and leaving funding for community projects on the table. History shows other counties will take advantage of this lack of foresight and benefit.

item.title: Nine million jobs are in limbo, and Congress can fix it before Christmas
item.description: If the American Franchise Act doesn't pass before this Congress adjourns, it dies, and the whole process starts over leaving owners in legal limbo.
item.content:encoded:
Ask most Americans who owns the McDonald's on the corner, the Holiday Inn off the interstate, or the gym down the street, and they'll tell you it's a big corporation. They're wrong. Most of those businesses are owned by local entrepreneurs who put their own savings on the line, sign the lease, make the payroll, and live in the town they serve. There are roughly 832,000 of these franchise small businesses in America, and together they support about nine million jobs.

Yet for more than a decade, Washington hasn't been able to answer a simple question for them: Who is the employer?

The answer has flipped with every change in administration. In 2015, the Obama labor board's Browning-Ferris decision blew up decades of precedent and said a parent brand could be on the hook for a franchisee's workers based on "indirect" or even unused control. A 2020 rule restored common sense. In 2023, the Biden board went further than Browning-Ferris, declaring that merely reserving the right to control was enough, before a federal court struck that rule down. The standard has now changed four times since 2015, and another court case could change it again in the next few months. No small-business owner can plan a five-year expansion around a rule that changes every four.

CHICK-FIL-A IS ONE OF AMERICA'S TOUGHEST FRANCHISES, AND THE STARTUP COST MAY SHOCK YOU

This isn't an abstract legal fight. When the International Franchise Association and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce studied the damage from the expanded standard, they found it cost the economy $33.3 billion a year, led to as many as 376,000 fewer job opportunities, and drove a 93% increase in lawsuits against franchise businesses. Ninety-two percent of the brands and owners surveyed said the rule meant less support from their brand.

That last number is the one that should bother Congress most. Under a sprawling joint-employer test, every bit of help a franchisor gives — a training program, an HR template, a workplace-safety manual — becomes evidence that it is really the boss. So the brands pull back. The national company with the lawyers and the compliance staff protects itself. The owner of three sandwich shops is left on her own. A rule sold as protecting workers ends up kneecapping the small employers who hire them.

The fix is sitting in front of Congress right now. The American Franchise Act (H.R. 5267 / S. 3525) writes one permanent, franchise-specific standard into federal law under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act. A franchisor would be a joint employer only if it both possesses and exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over essential terms of employment like wages, hiring, and scheduling. Setting brand standards, offering training, or requiring safety qualifications would not, by themselves, make a franchisor the employer. That is how franchising worked for most of its history, and it is how it should work.

Most important, it would be the law — not a board decision that the next administration can toss out on a party-line vote.

This is that rarest of things in Washington: a genuinely bipartisan bill. It was introduced by seven Republicans and seven Democrats. It has 158 cosponsors in the House, cleared the House Education and Workforce Committee in July, and has the backing of the White House. Members like Rep. Kevin Hern of Oklahoma, who owned and operated McDonald's restaurants before he came to Congress, understand from the inside what it means to meet a payroll under rules that won't sit still.

REP ROGER WILLIAMS: 250 YEARS OF HARD WORK PAYS OFF FOR MAIN STREET BUSINESSES

At Unleash Prosperity Now, our new paper, "Nine Million Jobs at Stake: Why Franchising Needs Regulatory Certainty," lays out what's on the line. One in eight American businesses with at least one employee is a franchise, and nearly two-thirds of local franchise owners are first-time business owners. This year alone, franchising is projected to create more than 150,000 new jobs. The conclusion is plain: Clarity is the cheapest pro-growth policy Congress can pass. It would also lift a compliance headache off small-business owners and free them to keep prices down at a moment when Americans have made clear that affordability is what they care about most. It doesn't cost the Treasury a dime, and it lets hundreds of thousands of small employers get back to hiring.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The clock matters. If the American Franchise Act doesn't pass before this Congress adjourns, it dies, and the whole process starts over, with a future labor board free to swing the pendulum back again. Franchise owners have already spent 10 years in limbo. They shouldn't be made to wait for another election cycle.

The lame-duck session is usually remembered for what Congress fails to do. Here's a chance to do something useful for Main Street before Christmas. Pass the American Franchise Act.

item.title: Georgia officer shoots 13-year-old after traffic stop linked to earlier shooting, police say
item.description: A 13-year-old suspected in a Jones County, Georgia, shooting was later wounded by a Milledgeville Police officer during a traffic stop at Milledgeville Mall, police say.
item.content:encoded:
A Georgia police officer shot and wounded a 13-year-old Sunday night while conducting a traffic stop linked to an earlier shooting, according to authorities.

The teenager is suspected of being involved in a Jones County robbery and shooting that left one man with a gunshot wound.

Jones County Sheriff Butch Reece said the teenager had met with four men from Macon for a gun sale on Etheridge Road when the group allegedly tried to rob the teenager. The teenager then opened fire, shooting one of the men.

GEORGIA DEPUTY FIRED AFTER HARASSING MOM WITH FAKE FACEBOOK PAGE

Authorities said the teenager fled the scene before being tracked down to the Milledgeville Mall parking lot, where Milledgeville police attempted to stop a vehicle determined to be linked to the Jones County shooting.

During the traffic stop, an officer shot the teenager, who sustained a single gunshot wound, Milledgeville Police said. A firearm was also recovered at the scene.

The teenager was alert, conscious and speaking following the shooting and was transported to a Macon-area hospital for medical treatment, where the juvenile was listed in stable condition, Milledgeville police said.

THREE TEENS, ADULT CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER WOMAN FINDS HER TEENAGE SON DEAD IN ABANDONED HOME

The circumstances surrounding the shooting were not immediately clear, including whether the teenager attempted to shoot the officer.

Milledgeville police said the Georgia Bureau of Investigation has been asked to respond and will take over the investigation.

item.title: Inside the Thanksgiving turkey hotline that's been saving holiday dinners for 45 years
item.description: From frozen turkeys to memorable phone calls, the experts behind Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line share how the Thanksgiving hotline has evolved over 45 seasons.
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving dinner can bring plenty of questions, especially when a frozen turkey, a crowded kitchen and hungry guests are involved. But for 45 seasons, Americans have had somewhere to turn when holiday cooking doesn't go according to plan.

Inside Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line in suburban Chicago, dozens of culinary professionals spend the holiday season helping home cooks with everything from thawing their turkeys to figuring out whether dinner is ready to serve.

The operation began in 1981 with just six female home economists answering calls by telephone, using a Rolodex to help guide their conversations.

"When the talk line started, it was just a mere six all-female home economists," said Nicole Johnson, director of the Turkey Talk-Line. "They were manning all of the phone calls, kind of old school Rolodex."

AFFORDABLE FOOD IDEAS AND TURKEY TIPS FOR THANKSGIVING THIS YEAR

Today, the team has grown to more than 50 chefs, dietitians and food scientists who answer thousands of questions each holiday season. While the telephone remains part of the operation, home cooks can now reach experts through text messages, email, online chat and social media.

The questions have evolved, too. Johnson said callers aren't always standing in front of an oven. Some reach out while shopping for Thanksgiving groceries, with the sound of shopping carts in the background as experts help them decide what to buy.

Others need advice about side dishes, ham or which meat thermometer to use. Home cooks can even send photos when they're having trouble explaining a problem.

Preparing to answer such a wide range of questions takes practice. Each October, the team goes through training known as Butterball University, testing cooking techniques and reviewing common holiday challenges. That includes some less conventional methods, such as cooking an entire turkey in the microwave.

The experts also experiment with recipes in a test kitchen, including ways to use Thanksgiving leftovers.

THANKSGIVING DAY RECIPES

The annual preparation comes as more Americans say they plan to cook their own holiday centerpiece. New research from FMI – The Food Industry Association found 59% of shoppers planning to serve turkey expect to prepare it from scratch this year, up from 43% in 2025.

Regardless of experience, one question comes up repeatedly: How long does it take to thaw a turkey?

Experts recommend allowing about 24 hours in the refrigerator for every four pounds, meaning a 20-pound turkey needs roughly five days to thaw. For cooks running short on time, cold-water thawing takes approximately 30 minutes per pound, with the water changed every half hour. The turkey should be cooked immediately afterward.

But answering questions isn't always as straightforward as providing a cooking time or temperature. 

"We're turkey counselors, we're turkey detectives," said Bill Nolan, a retired chef and culinary educator who has worked on the Talk-Line for 10 seasons.

Nolan said callers sometimes reach out in a panic, leaving experts to piece together what went wrong before they can offer a solution.

'FOOD BABE' DECLARES WAR ON THE 'HOLIDAY DEATH AISLE' AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING

And after a decade of conversations, some have stayed with him for reasons that have little to do with cooking.

"A gentleman called up, he had lost his wife, and he wanted to cook dinner for his family and his grandkids, and he'd never done it," Nolan recalled. "And I took the time to walk him through the process."

"It's those types of calls that really hit you right here," he added.

The Talk-Line continues operating through Dec. 24, with experts available at 1-800-BUTTERBALL or by text at 844-877-3456.

item.title: In a world of surging hacks and attacks, is anyone running the show?
item.description: As hackers hit 178 companies and the FBI suffered its second breach since September, White House messaging on the outages took a full week to recover.
item.content:encoded:
Most of America is feeling a deep-seated anxiety about the outages and the hacking and the ground stop and the banking blackout and the dark and growing threat of AI.

Yeah, I'm not immune to it either.

Some panicky types are even stocking up on food, fearing the worst.

All this reminds me of a New York Post headline in the fall of 1990.

LAWMAKERS WARN AMERICANS OF VULNERABLE SYSTEMS AMID STREAK OF OUTAGES: 'SOMETHING IS GOING ON'

In his first year as New York City's first Black mayor, David Dinkins faced a wave of violent crime and high-profile murders. The courtly Dinkins was seen as too passive in his response.

And so the tabloid screamed: "DAVE, DO SOMETHING!"

It didn't matter what. He just needed to reassure the frightened citizenry that he was taking some kind of action.

PRESIDENT TRUMP DOWNPLAYS PANIC OVER TECH OUTAGES: ‘NOBODY’S GOING TO PLAY GAMES WITH US’

I believe — and this is not a partisan observation — that the sense (fairly or unfairly) that no one has their hand on the rocky wheel has boosted the unsettled feelings in the country.

Part of that is President Trump's style. He tends to minimize threats and concerns in dismissive fashion. Nothing to see here. It's all unconnected. Relax.

DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

"It's life," he said. "When you're big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine."

This is just life in the modern technological age. Stuff happens.

I'd say it took a full week for White House officials to get it through their skulls that their messaging was an absolute disaster.

It didn't help that Trump was in China, causing his own uproar with his friendly words about the world's leading Communist dictators, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. But it's unfair to blame the president for being on the long-scheduled trip, as he wanted, with basically no success, to talk about curbing nuclear weapons.

SWIFT ASSURANCES FROM OFFICIALS AFTER WAVE OF NATIONWIDE OUTAGES RAISES QUESTIONS, EXPERT SAYS

The initial mess back home got muddier in the hands of Markwayne Mullin, who may be a good Homeland Security secretary but is awful on television.

He said he had spoken to "one guy who is very smart with tech" — this from an official with all the resources of the government — who told him AI might be behind the recent outages. Another time, Mullin said he was "98%" sure the outages were not part of a terrorist attack.

MULLIN TOOK GOVERNMENT PLANE TO LSU-TEXAS FOOTBALL GAME WITH AMERICANS STRANDED IN WAKE OF FAA OUTAGE: REPORT

And talk about a tin ear: When the FAA ground stop stranded millions of Americans, many sleeping in terminals, Mullin took a government jet to see the LSU-Texas game — and sat with the CEO of Louisiana's Bollinger Shipyards, which holds more than $2 billion in DHS contracts.

Mullin defended the trip by saying he was required to fly on federal planes and reimbursed the government. Marco Rubio has repeatedly done the same thing to watch his son play football. But Mullin's failure to recognize the terrible timing is beyond stunning.

NSA'S HIGHLY CLASSIFIED COMMUNICATIONS NETWORK DISRUPTED BY WIDESPREAD OUTAGE

When Stephen Miller pulled Mullin off TV, the White House leaked a story to Breitbart about the brilliance of the move. "This speaks to Stephen’s ability to flawlessly manage a crisis," an unnamed White House official said of the new chief of staff.

But Miller actually waited way too long. He had put out a memo saying Cabinet departments could manage their own media strategy. By the time he pulled the plug on Mullin, the damage had been done. Susie Wiles, who believed in central control, would have benched the guy after the first fumble.

It was not until last Wednesday that the powers that be apparently realized how damaging the who’s-in-charge narrative had become. Minutes before JD Vance was to take the stage at The New York Times DealBook summit, he canceled, with the explanation that he had to return to Washington to lead meetings on the seemingly nonstop outages.

But this was drowned out by the cascade of bad news. Hackers last week attacked 178 companies — including CNN, BBC and Zoom — and made it look easy. The FBI was hacked on Friday, the second breach since September. That day, an outage at the super-secret National Security Agency, and its classified communications network, was finally fixed.

All this wasn’t just a messaging problem for the administration, but a failure to perform.

Sean Duffy, the Transportation secretary, was known primarily for his reality show background (MTV's "The Real World"), and the ex-congressman spent weeks this summer filming a family trip across America that might have been devoted to the crumbling FAA infrastructure.

In fairness, Joe Biden's guy, Pete Buttigieg, was an ex-mayor and former presidential candidate with no special expertise on transportation issues.

Others who held the job were politically connected insiders or senators, House members and governors: Elizabeth Dole. Elaine Chao. Norm Mineta. Andrew Card. Neil Goldschmidt. Brock Adams.

The national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, a former top official at the Republican National Committee, was pushed out late last week. "I didn’t think that person was good enough," the president said. Suddenly, actual expertise is at a premium.

Trump tried one of his go-to moves, blaming everything on Biden. But it turns out the former president pushed through a bipartisan measure that included $25 billion for improving airports and air traffic control infrastructure. Trump says the money was "spent unwisely," and Duffy has asked for another $50 billion.

"We have to get the money," Trump said, to repair an "obsolete" system.

Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill last year included $12.5 billion to modernize the air traffic control system, but part of that money remains unspent.

For all the blame-shifting and finger-pointing, it’s not hard to imagine a modern-day version of that headline: "DONALD, DO SOMETHING!"

The administration is trying. The Democrats who take over Congress will be under similar pressure.

The problem is that an old and rickety system that was largely ignored for decades can’t be fixed with a snap of the fingers.

FOLLOW US ON X

Throw in hacking, foreign cyberattacks and rogue AI networks, and it’s no wonder many Americans have the sense that no one is in charge.

But let’s look at the country-in-crisis theme from a slightly different perspective.

Late last week, the release of "Grand Theft Auto 6" generated nearly $4 billion in sales by the first day. It was probably the biggest launch of any creative work in entertainment history, Axios says.

After waiting 13 years for an update, gamers ordered 32 million copies at 80 bucks apiece.

GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS

Reviewers absolutely swooned over the video game, calling it unbelievable, astonishing, a cultural atlas of American life — a "masterpiece," as Bloomberg put it.

SEND US A TIP

While there is some debate over the central characters, Jason and Lucia, small-time crooks who sometimes kill people and commit other dirty deeds, it’s almost universally described as addictive.

GOT A TIP?

Does that sound like a country that is wallowing in fear? The same goes for the passionate debate over Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond, cast by one outraged fan as the "worst decision in all of cinema history."

What I draw from this is that diversions and distractions still rule. The uneasiness over outages and outrages, over gas and grocery prices, is not yet a fully formed freak-out. That could change with further hacks and attacks, but for most people, life goes on.

item.title: NFL replay booth wipes out Jaguars' Parker Washington touchdown in upset loss to Giants
item.description: Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville Jaguars lost a disputed Parker Washington touchdown catch to NFL replay in a 23-18 defeat by the New York Giants.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants upset the Jacksonville Jaguars 23-18 on Sunday, courtesy of a fourth-quarter goal-line stand from the NFL replay booth.

Trailing 20-6 early in the fourth quarter, Jaguars QB Trevor Lawrence fired toward wide receiver Parker Washington in the back corner of the end zone.

Washington went up, snagged the ball, switched hands midair and got both feet down before falling out of bounds. Officials waved it incomplete anyway. With a chance to make it a one-score game on the line, Jaguars coach Liam Coen threw the challenge flag.

SEAN MCVAY SAYS NFL HAS ADMITTED OFFICIALS MADE MAJOR MISTAKE THAT PROBABLY COST THE RAMS A LOSS VS DENVER

The replay looked like six points to almost everyone watching, from fans at home to analysts in the booth. The league office saw it differently, letting the call stand and keeping Jacksonville out of the end zone.

Postgame, NFL replay vice president Mark Butterworth noted that the booth lacked clear and obvious evidence to overturn the call.

Because the ball shifted when Washington hit the turf, replay officials ruled he never established control until he was out of bounds.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That conflicted with what Jacksonville heard on the sideline. Coen said officials blamed the call on Washington switching hands mid-catch.

Giants coach John Harbaugh kept it simple, saying the ball moved.

FORMER NFL QB SEAN SALISBURY WANTS OFFICIALS TO FACE POSTGAME QUESTIONS JUST LIKE PLAYERS AND COACHES

Even Giants safety Jevon Holland admitted postgame he thought Washington had him beat:

"The game's over ... that might have been a catch. That was a hell of a play. I thought he got his foot down, I was like, 'Damn.' But then they called it out and I was like, 'S--t, all right.' Shout-out Vegas. I don't know."

Instead of cutting the deficit to seven, Jacksonville settled for a field goal to make it 20-9, a four-point swing in a five-point game.

In the locker room, Jacksonville skipped the excuses.

"I felt good about it, but they said it wasn’t a catch, so had to move on and finish that game," Washington said after watching the replay on the stadium video board.

Replay drama aside, New York won this game up front. Giants linebacker Abdul Carter wrecked Jacksonville's protection, piling up two sacks, two tackles for loss, five QB hits and eight pressures.

The nonstop heat from the Giants' defensive line rattled Lawrence, who finished 25-of-47 for 301 yards and two picks. He took a beating, yet led a late touchdown drive to pull within five before time ran out.

New York escaped to protect its division lead.

Between Carter wrecking the pocket and the replay booth wiping six points off the board, Jacksonville flew home empty-handed.

item.title: Lions' Jameson Williams does front flip touchdown celebration one week after Aidan Hutchinson's injury
item.description: Jameson Williams' 57-yard touchdown front flip drew fan backlash after Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson's knee injury in Germany ended his season.
item.content:encoded:
Aidan Hutchinson’s sack celebration, where he jumped in the air and threw his fist up in Germany in an ode to its soccer culture, unfortunately ended the Detroit Lions’ star’s season after suffering a knee injury.

So, surely Hutchinson’s injury would be a PSA on what not to do when celebrating a big play, right?

Well, his Lions teammate, wide receiver Jameson Williams, might not have caught that memo when he decided to do a front flip while crossing the goal line for a 57-yard touchdown in the Lions’ win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at home.

As you might expect, Williams caught flak from football fans for the celebration, which in usual times may look harmless.

But considering what just happened to his team’s defensive captain just last week, and how it wasn’t a clean landing in the end zone, it wasn’t the best of decisions.

After the game, Williams spoke with ESPN’s Lindsey Thiry, who asked the veteran receiver if head coach Dan Campbell said anything about the celebration.

"Yeah," he replied, "I tried to land it. I didn’t really know what to do, so I just did a front flip."

So, no more … right?

"I’m going to try to land one later in the year for y’all, for sure" he added.

Okay, then.

Again, we’ve seen many flip celebrations throughout the NFL over the years. New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo, who promised he wouldn’t be doing his signature back flip anymore after seeing Hutchinson’s injury, couldn’t help himself when picking up the game-winning first down against the Jacksonville Jaguars hours after Williams’ own flip.

Emotions can take over in a game, and these elite athletes like to show off their skills when warranted.

item.title: San Francisco 49ers lineman Colton McKivitz suffers injury so gruesome players from both teams turn away
item.description: Colton McKivitz suffered a gruesome ankle injury in Mexico City after his leg was trapped in a pileup, as teammates refused to look and he was carted off.
item.content:encoded:
NFL players are used to football's violence and the price that sometimes must be paid in the currency of pain and injuries. So, when a player is injured in such a manner that players refuse to look at their fallen teammate or opponent, you know it's terrible.

That is exactly what played out with San Francisco 49ers right tackle Colton McKivitz during the 35-10 victory against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City on Sunday night.

During a second-quarter run to the right, McKivitz was caught in a pileup and his left leg was caught beneath other players.

CHIEFS' TYQUAN THORNTON DIDN'T REALIZE HIS FOOT WAS POINTING THE WRONG DIRECTION AFTER GAME-CHANGING CATCH

LIONS' STAR HURT CELEBRATING SACK OF PATRIOTS’ DRAKE MAYE AS BOTH INJURED ON POSSIBLY SEASON-ALTERING PLAY

And his leg was pointing in one direction and his foot was pointing in a different direction at a greater than 90-degree angle.

Players immediately sank to their knees or crouched, most facing away from the gruesome injury.

Even game officials looked away and shook their heads.

San Francisco left tackle Trent Williams walked over to his fallen teammate, who was clutching at his lower leg. And when the injury came into focus, Williams took off his helmet and slammed it to the turf in frustration, empathy and perhaps pity.

Trainers and other medical officials rushed to McKivitz and eventually loaded him on a cart to take him away to the locker room at Estadio Banorte.

TEARS FROM TEAMMATES AS IMMOBILIZED DETROIT LIONS LINEBACKER JACK CAMPBELL CARTED OFF FIELD AND HOSPITALIZED

By that time, the trainers had placed a compression brace on McKivitz and the injury was no longer visible. That's when teammates surrounded the cart McKivitz was on and paid their respects to their fallen teammate.

It was a horrible scene from start to finish.

They scored a touchdown on a Mike Evans one-handed touchdown grab. And scored again on a Pick Six interception by Ji'Ayir Brown.

item.title: Trump's Thanksgiving turkeys arrive at luxury DC hotel as Americans vote on their names
item.description: Two turkeys raised on a West Virginia farm strutted a red carpet at the Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., ahead of Tuesday's pardon.
item.content:encoded:
Talk about talking turkey.

Two feathered VIPs have checked into one of Washington's most luxurious hotels, complete with plush beds, a red-carpet welcome and a crowd of eager photographers, ahead of President Donald Trump's annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House.

The presidential hopefuls arrived Sunday at the historic Willard InterContinental Washington, D.C., where they were photographed strutting across a red carpet, posing for pictures and standing atop the hotel's beds before their big day on the South Lawn.

THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION

The U.S. Department of Agriculture celebrated their arrival on X, announcing a "SPECIAL DELIVERY TO WASHINGTON, D.C.!" and describing the birds as "two VERY special guests" receiving the presidential treatment.

Photographs shared by the USDA, credited to the White House and National Turkey Federation, showed the plump white birds making their grand entrance before an audience of hotel guests and photographers. One turkey was even pictured riding through the hotel's ornate hallways inside a travel crate perched on a brass luggage cart.

The pair appeared equally comfortable with the accommodations, with one bird spreading its feathers atop a neatly made bed while its companion stood nearby.

But before the turkeys meet the commander in chief, Americans have been invited to settle a pressing matter of national importance: What should they be called?

SOCIAL MEDIA USERS ARE EATING HUGE AMOUNTS OF CARROTS AND SHRIMP FOR A NATURAL TAN

The White House launched an online contest offering three possible combinations: "Commander & Chief," "Freedom & Feathers" and "Honey & Ham."

Voting on the names closed Sunday at 5 p.m. ET, with the winning pair expected to be announced before a second round of voting opens Monday at 8 a.m. That final vote will determine which turkey receives the official ceremonial pardon.

The birds, raised by American turkey farmers Scott and Becky Rightsell at Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, have already received their own playful presidential biographies.

Both hatched July 15, but their tastes apparently differ. According to the White House, one enjoys Golden Delicious apples and scenic country drives, while the other prefers Dr Pepper and dreams of vacationing in Aggieland.

The pair was selected from a larger flock based on appearance and temperament, according to West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey's office. Their preparations included getting accustomed to crowds, camera lights and noise.

And for Americans who cannot get enough turkey-related excitement, the White House has unveiled "Gobble Getaway," an online game challenging players to help a turkey dodge a chef armed with a net and roasting pan while making its way across the South Lawn to the pardon podium.

The annual Thanksgiving tradition dates back to 1947, when the National Turkey Federation first presented a holiday bird to President Harry Truman.

FOX NEWS MEDIA KICKS OFF HOLIDAY SEASON WITH SEVENTH ANNUAL ALL-AMERICAN CHRISTMAS TREE LIGHTING

President John F. Kennedy spared a gift turkey in 1963, while President George H.W. Bush established the formal presidential turkey pardon in 1989.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are scheduled to participate in this year's ceremony on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2 p.m. ET on the White House South Lawn.

Although the public gets to vote on which turkey receives the ceremonial pardon, both birds are traditionally spared the Thanksgiving dinner table.

For now, the pair can enjoy their luxury accommodations and newfound celebrity status, knowing their next stop is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue rather than the oven.

item.title: John Malkovich recalls losing 'pretty much everything' to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme
item.description: John Malkovich opens up to "60 Minutes" about losing his entire fortune to Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme and the moment he told his wife the news.
item.content:encoded:
John Malkovich recalled once losing his entire fortune to disgraced financier Bernie Madoff.

Malkovich, 72, told "60 Minutes" that he had recently returned from directing a play in Mexico City when he found out about Madoff's Ponzi scheme.

"I got home from that and I saw this photograph of Bernie Madoff in handcuffs, and I thought, 'Oh, well that could prove interesting,'" Malkovich said. "I went in and said to my wife, you know, 'I'm just going to go around the corner, buy a pack of cigarettes.'"

FRAUD MASTERMIND BEHIND MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR PONZI SCHEME THAT VICTIMIZED TRAVIS KELCE IS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT

He added, "I said, 'We have a little problem. Bernie Madoff just got arrested.'"

Malkovich, a previous smoker, hadn't indulged in nicotine "for a while" when he left the house that day, he said.

"That was pretty much everything I'd ever made," he admitted before coming to terms with his situation. "You know, you look to blame, you're going to do this and that, and then you realize, 'Look, why don't you shut up?'"

FORMER DISNEY STAR ERIK VON DETTEN SUED FOR ELDER ABUSE AFTER COUPLE POURED $2.1M RETIREMENT SAVINGS INTO GOLD

"Whatever you lost, most people who were ever born will never have a 10th of that, no matter what they do. No matter what they do. Get on with your life and that's it."

Madoff died in April 2021 while serving a 150-year sentence at the federal medical care center in Butner, North Carolina, where his attorney said he was being treated for terminal kidney failure.

A decades-long force on Wall Street, Madoff shocked the world when he pleaded guilty in 2009 to running a vast Ponzi scheme that prosecutors said swindled thousands out of their life savings. The scheme began in the early 1970s, and by the time Madoff was arrested in December 2008, had defrauded as many as 37,000 people in 136 countries out of up to $65 billion. 

His victims included the famous – director Steven Spielberg, actor Kevin Bacon and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel – as well as ordinary investors.

Madoff said he started the fraud, in which he appeared to deliver steady returns to clients, but was actually using money from new investors to pay off existing shareholders, in the 1990s because he felt "compelled" to give investors solid returns despite the recession and weak stock market. Prosecutors contend he started defrauding investors much earlier.

"When I began the Ponzi scheme, I believed it would end shortly and I would be able to extricate myself and my clients," Madoff told the judge at his plea hearing. "However, this proved difficult, and ultimately impossible, and as the years went by, I realized that my arrest and this day would inevitably come."

Prior to his downfall, Madoff was viewed as a self-made and respected figure among financial professionals as the head of the seemingly successful Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities firm. He also served as the chairman of the Nasdaq Stock Market in 1990, 1991 and 1993.

In addition to being sentenced to the maximum 150 years in prison, Madoff and his family took a major financial hit: A judge issued a $171 billion forfeiture order in June 2009 requiring the disgraced financier to give up his interests in all property, including real estate, investments, cars and boats. Under the arrangement, the government also obtained his wife's interest in all property, including $80 million that she claimed belonged to her, leaving Ruth Madoff with $2.5 million in assets.

The decline and fall of Madoff also took a toll on his family. The oldest of his two sons, Mark Madoff, died by suicide on the second anniversary of his father's arrest in 2010. His other son, Andrew, died from cancer at age 48 in 2014.

Mark Madoff's suicide prompted his mother, Ruth Madoff, to cut off all communications with her husband.

"I was responsible for my son Mark's death and that's very, very difficult," Madoff said during a 2013 interview with CNN. "I live with that. I live with the remorse, the pain I caused everybody, certainly my family, and the victims."

item.title: Man convicted for role in Tessa Majors' 2019 NYC killing released on parole
item.description: Luchiano Lewis, convicted in the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors, was freed on conditional parole after serving fewer than seven years behind bars.
item.content:encoded:
One of the three then-teenagers convicted in connection with the 2019 murder of Barnard College freshman Tessa Majors in New York City has now been released on conditional parole supervision, according to the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision.

Luchiano Lewis, now 21, was released on Oct. 14 under conditional release and placed under community supervision after serving fewer than seven years behind bars for his role in the robbery and killing in Manhattan's Morningside Park in December 2019, state correction records show.

Lewis, who was released from the Franklin Correctional Facility, had been sentenced to nine years to life after pleading guilty in 2021 to second-degree murder and first-degree robbery in connection with Majors' killing.

MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE

Under New York State law, Lewis' conditional release did not require him to go before the State Board of Parole because eligible inmates can qualify for conditional release after serving two-thirds of their minimum sentence, subject to applicable requirements and good-time allowances.

Majors, who was 18 when she was killed, was attacked on Dec. 11, 2019, near a staircase in Morningside Park.

Prosecutors said a group of teens confronted Majors in an attempted robbery, during which she was stabbed multiple times. She was eventually able to climb a set of stairs and reach the street before collapsing. She was taken to a hospital, where she died from her injuries.

JUDGE SENTENCES LILY PETERS' KILLER 4 YEARS AFTER 10-YEAR-OLD FOUND DEAD IN WOODS

After the crime, then-14-year-old Lewis and another 14-year-old were both tried as adults for the attack. Prosecutors said Lewis held Majors in a headlock while the other 14-year-old stabbed her multiple times.

While Lewis was not holding the knife in the attack, prosecutors said he played a key role in the robbery that killed Majors.

At Lewis' sentencing, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Robert Mandelbaum said the killing "tore at the fabric of the entire city."

"The defendant was and is extremely young. He has his whole life ahead of him, but Tessa Majors does not," he added.

Majors' parents described the lasting impact of the loss of their child during Lewis' sentencing, remembering her as a talented student, musician and writer whose future was tragically ended too soon.

The two other teenagers convicted in connection with the killing — Rashaun Weaver, who was 14 at the time of the crime, and Zyairr Davis, who was 13 at the time — remain behind bars. Weaver was sentenced to 14 years to life in prison for murder and robbery, while Davis pleaded guilty to robbery and was sentenced to 18 months in juvenile detention. Davis completed his juvenile sentence but is now being held on an unrelated attempted murder case.

item.title: New York Dem addresses bizarre 'lizard people' claims after viral clip behind Mamdani
item.description: New York Assemblyman Jordan J.G. Wright breaks silence on viral reptilian claims after a clip showed him rolling his eyes behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic New York City assemblyman addressed bizarre "lizard people" conspiracy theories after a viral video appeared to show his eyes rolling backward while standing behind Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a press conference.

Jordan J.G. Wright was spotted during a press conference behind Mamdani on Friday, when the city announced plans to eventually shut down Rikers Island.

As Mamdani spoke, Wright appeared to flash a slight grin before blinking and rolling his eyes in a circular motion toward the back of his head, prompting a wave of bizarre speculation online.

"I have no idea what was going on in that video. I’m really not sure," Wright told the New York Post in a statement.

NYC MAYOR MAMDANI ANNOUNCES DELAYED PLAN TO CLOSE CITY'S LARGEST JAIL

He added that his work as an assemblyman speaks to his human character, pointing to a project he championed in Harlem that serves as the city's first community-based center dedicated to climate action. The five-story hub provides residents with environmental education and advocacy.

"Obviously I’m a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he said. "I can’t speak to any reptiles or aliens."

The video sent social media users into a frenzy over the weekend, reigniting a decades-old conspiracy theory that extraterrestrial reptilians secretly control the Earth by disguising themselves as world leaders and celebrities to manipulate society.

"This is how lizards blink… I am pretty sure there is full-blown ‘Men in Black’ aliens walking among us disguised as human beings, and they are hiding in plain sight," one social media user said, according to the Post.

NYC SUSPECT IN CHINATOWN FATAL BEATING HAD 5 OPEN CASES AS MAMDANI PUSHES PLAN TO CLOSE RIKERS

Another X user suggested the clip showed that aliens were becoming increasingly brazen about revealing themselves to the public.

"The ‘reptile’ is standing right behind Mamdani, as he announces a full scale-release of dangerous prisoners from NYC jails," the X user said.

"The aliens are not even bothering to hide themselves anymore. They intend to create so much chaos on Earth, that we will be unable to defend ourselves," the user added.

The discussion also spilled onto Reddit, where some users questioned whether Wright was human.

"Yes, the guy in the back is a reptilian, 100%" the Reddit user said.

MAMDANI IGNITES ONLINE FIRESTORM AFTER MOURNING DEATH OF INMATE CHARGED IN GRISLY MURDER: 'WTF ARE WE DOING?'

Wright, the son of former Assemblyman Keith L.T. Wright and grandson of former New York Supreme Court Judge Bruce Wright, represents New York's 70th Assembly District in Harlem.

He was reelected without opposition in November after defeating Democratic socialist Conrad Blackburn in the Democratic primary in June. His legislative priorities include affordable housing, health care access and public safety, according to his profile.

A lifelong New Yorker and Central Harlem resident, Wright graduated from Syracuse University in 2017 with a degree in psychology.

Wright stood behind Mamdani on Friday as the mayor announced plans to cut New York City's jail population by 2,500 inmates over the next five years and close the city’s largest jail by 2032.

The remaining inmates, estimated at 4,100 detainees, will be moved to four new, smaller borough-based jails opening in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx.

Fox News Digital reached out to Jordan J.G. Wright for comment.

item.title: Cam Skattebo ignores his own backflip celebration retirement promise at end of Giants victory over Jaguars
item.description: Cam Skattebo vowed to retire his backflip celebration, then did one anyway after the New York Giants clinched their 23-18 win over Jacksonville.
item.content:encoded:
There are some things about Cam Skattebo that the New York Giants can definitely count on: he is going to bring energy, he's still in danger of fumbling and he should not be trusted when he says he's going to put the backflip on the back burner.

Two of those three are not optimal.

One of those three is really moronic.

LIONS' STAR HURT CELEBRATING SACK OF PATRIOTS’ DRAKE MAYE AS BOTH INJURED ON POSSIBLY SEASON-ALTERING PLAY

CAM SKATTEBO PUTTING HIS BACKFLIP ON THE BACK BURNER AFTER SEEING AIDAN HUTCHINSON CELEBRATION INJURY

Days after telling reporters he was going to retire from his signature backflip celebration, Skattebo apparently decided to ignore everything he said (good advice for all of us, actually) and performed one of his semi-plyometric flights near the end of the Giants game on Sunday.

"When energy calls for it, it calls for it," Skattebo boldly explained to reporters after the game. "My teammates, I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team and play this game with my heart and soul. So when that happens, it's second nature.

"It's hard to hold back."

You want to know the dumb part about this explanation? Neither energy, nor the team were calling for Skattebo to perform a backflip at the moment he did.

The Giants had clinched their 23-18 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars with two minutes to play when Skattebo delivered a 5-yard run. The game was effectively over.

But that's when Skattebo forgot everything he said about not risking an injury the way he watched Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson did on Nov. 15 – which was by leaving his feet to perform a celebration.

DAN CAMPBELL WON'T STOP PLAYERS FROM CELEBRATING EVEN AFTER STAR AIDAN HUTCHINSON WAS INJURED CELEBRATING

Hutchinson, by the way, last week promised he's done going airborne.

So, Skattebo did his unretired backflip when the game was decided. And wouldn't it have been utterly embarrassing if he'd done that backflip upon clinching a victory, injured himself needlessly, and been unable to play in the coming weeks?

Skattebo had coach John Harbaugh previously convinced he had gained some wisdom after the coach read the player's quotes about his backflip last Friday.

Harbaugh actually said in a press conference he was thinking of discussing the matter with Skattebo, but decided it wasn't necessary because the running back seemed to understand the celebration might not be in his or the team's best interest.

But, nope.

Skattebo in the air, feet above his head, relying on his feet and ankles to hold up during the landing and hoping his knees don't buckle.

So, a conversation with Harbaugh is likely incoming.

Skattebo is obviously valuable to the Giants. It's the reason they're not thrilled with these backflips in the first place.

But while he's important to the team, he's also kind of just a solid player. If he weren't playing in New York, the chances of him being a marketing thing would be far smaller because, well, take Sunday as an example:

He rushed 14 times for 34 yards — a 2.4-yard-per-carry average.

He caught three passes for 14 yards.

And fumbled once, which he lost.

So the guy is solid. And hard to figure out. And something of a frustration for Harbaugh.
